# Shopping cart

A small CommonJS `ShoppingCart` class. It started as a buggy example with five known defects. This repo fixes them and adds regression tests.

## Usage

```js
const ShoppingCart = require('./src/cart');

const cart = new ShoppingCart();            // or new ShoppingCart({ decimalPlaces: 0 }) for JPY
cart.addItem('Coffee', 4.5, 2);
cart.addItem('Bagel', 2.25);                // quantity defaults to 1
cart.addItem('Coffee', 4.5, 1);             // merges into the existing line: quantity 3
cart.applyDiscount(20);                     // 20% off, replaces any earlier discount

cart.getTotal();                            // 12.6
cart.getItemCount();                        // 2 (distinct lines)
cart.removeItem('Bagel');                   // true
cart.removeItem('Bagel');                   // false, nothing to remove

cart.addItem('Refund', -5, 1);              // throws RangeError: price must be at least 0, received -5
cart.applyDiscount(150);                    // throws RangeError: discount percent must be at most 100, received 150
```

## Scripts

| Command                 | What it does                                                    |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm test`              | Runs every `tests/**/*.test.js` file with Node's built-in runner |
| `npm run test:coverage` | Same, with a line/branch/function coverage report               |
| `npm run lint`          | ESLint over the whole project                                   |

Requires Node 22 or newer. `npm test` has no dependencies. `npm run lint` needs `npm install` first.

## The five bugs

| # | Where          | Symptom in the original                                                                                                                         | Fix                                                                                                | Regression tests (grep for the name)                                                        |
| - | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1 | `addItem`      | Accepted negative prices and quantities, and also `NaN`, `Infinity` and strings, producing negative or `NaN` totals.                               | Validates name, price (finite, ≥ 0) and quantity (whole number, ≥ 1) before touching state.        | `Bug 1 regression: rejects negative or otherwise invalid price and quantity`                |
| 2 | `removeItem`   | `i.name = name` assigned instead of comparing. The filter callback returned the (truthy) name, so nothing was removed and every item was renamed. A missing item was ignored silently. | Compares with `===`. Returns `true` if a line was removed and `false` if none matched.              | `Bug 2 regression: removes only the named item…`, `…leaves the remaining items unmodified…`, `…returns false…when the item is missing` |
| 3 | `getTotal`     | `i <= this.items.length` read one element past the end, so `getTotal` threw a `TypeError` on every call, even for an empty cart.                  | Sums with `reduce`, so there is no index to get wrong.                                              | `Bug 3 regression: returns 0 for an empty cart…`, `…totals a single item…`                   |
| 4 | `getTotal`     | Added the discount: 10% off 100 returned 110.                                                                                                    | Subtracts it: `subtotal × (100 − percent) / 100`.                                                   | `Bug 4 regression: a 10% discount lowers a 100 total to 90, not 110`, `…25% discount…`       |
| 5 | `applyDiscount`| Accepted any value, so 150 produced a negative total and −20 a surcharge.                                                                         | Requires a finite number from 0 to 100 inclusive. A rejected call keeps the previous discount.     | `Bug 5 regression: rejects out-of-range and non-numeric discounts`                           |

The first commit on this branch is the original file, unchanged, so `git diff` against it shows exactly what changed. To check the tests, each bug was put back into the fixed code one at a time, and every time the tests named for that bug failed. Bug 3 also fails the discount tests, because they call `getTotal`.

ESLint's `no-return-assign` rule also flags Bug 2 in the original file.

## Design decisions

**Error types.** Wrong type → `TypeError` (`'5'` as a price, `null` as a name). Right type, bad value → `RangeError` (negative, `NaN`, `Infinity`, fractional quantity, blank name, discount over 100). Messages name the argument, the rule and the value received. Every check runs before any state changes, so a rejected call leaves the cart exactly as it was.

**`removeItem` returns a boolean instead of throwing.** A missing item is state, not bad input. This matches `Map#delete` and `Set#delete`, and makes a double-clicked "remove" button harmless. A non-string or blank name is a caller bug, so it still throws. Items are removed in place with `splice`, so a reference held to `cart.items` stays current.

**Money is computed in integer minor units.** `getTotal` converts the subtotal to cents, or whatever `decimalPlaces` says, and applies the discount in integers. It then rounds half up once and converts back. This keeps floating-point noise out of results: `0.1 × 3` returns `0.3`, not `0.30000000000000004`. Currency precision is configurable because it isn't always 2: `new ShoppingCart({ decimalPlaces: 0 })` for JPY, `3` for KWD. The limit is 8, because beyond that ordinary totals overflow `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. A total too large to represent exactly throws a `RangeError` instead of returning a wrong number.

Sub-cent unit prices are allowed. They are multiplied by quantity before rounding, so `0.125 × 1000` is exactly `125`. When one is combined with a discount, the value is rounded twice: once at the subtotal and once after the discount.

**Repeat adds keep the first price.** `addItem('Apple', 0.5)` followed by `addItem('Apple', 0.75)` gives one line at 0.5 with quantity 2. This is the original behaviour. Changing it wasn't part of the bug list, so it is kept and pinned by a test. To change a price, remove the item and add it again.

**Quantity defaults to 1.** The original signature had no default, and omitting the quantity produced `NaN`. Quantities must be whole numbers. Items sold by weight would need a different model.

**`getItemCount` counts distinct lines, not units.** This is unchanged from the original and documented in the JSDoc.

**Names match exactly.** Matching is case-sensitive, with no trimming and no Unicode normalization. `'Café'` written as one code point and as `e` + combining accent are two different items. Normalizing would quietly change the names callers passed in.

**`items`, `discount` and `decimalPlaces` are plain public properties.** The original exposed `items` and `discount`, and existing callers may read them. Validation happens in the methods. Writing to the properties directly bypasses it.

## Layout

```
src/cart.js         ShoppingCart class, the public entry point
src/validation.js   Argument checks shared by the cart methods
src/money.js        Minor-unit conversion, rounding and percent discount
tests/cart.test.js              Per-method behaviour, one regression group per bug, end-to-end flow
tests/cart.edge-cases.test.js   Numeric limits, unicode and odd names, large carts, instance isolation
tests/validation.test.js        Validator bounds and error messages
tests/money.test.js             Rounding and discount arithmetic
```

## Out of scope

- One algorithm for totals, not two. The guideline to implement two approaches is meant for real strategy choices, such as rate-limiting algorithms. For a cart total, a second approach would just be a way to get the same sum wrong.
- Concurrency. The cart is synchronous and single-threaded. Every method finishes before another can run, so there is nothing to interleave.

Sub-cent unit prices are allowed. They are multiplied by quantity before rounding, so `0.125 × 1000` is exactly `125`. When one is combined with a discount, the value is rounded twice: once at the subtotal and once after the discount.

**Repeat adds keep the first price.** `addItem('Apple', 0.5)` followed by `addItem('Apple', 0.75)` gives one line at 0.5 with quantity 2. This is the original behaviour. Changing it wasn't part of the bug list, so it is kept and pinned by a test. To change a price, remove the item and add it again.

**Quantity defaults to 1.** The original signature had no default, and omitting the quantity produced `NaN`. Quantities must be whole numbers. Items sold by weight would need a different model.

**`getItemCount` counts distinct lines, not units.** This is unchanged from the original and documented in the JSDoc.

**Names match exactly.** Matching is case-sensitive, with no trimming and no Unicode normalization. `'Café'` written as one code point and as `e` + combining accent are two different items. Normalizing would quietly change the names callers passed in.

**`items`, `discount` and `decimalPlaces` are plain public properties.** The original exposed `items` and `discount`, and existing callers may read them. Validation happens in the methods. Writing to the properties directly bypasses it.

## Layout

```
src/cart.js         ShoppingCart class, the public entry point
src/validation.js   Argument checks shared by the cart methods
src/money.js        Minor-unit conversion, rounding and percent discount
tests/cart.test.js              Per-method behaviour, one regression group per bug, end-to-end flow
tests/cart.edge-cases.test.js   Numeric limits, unicode and odd names, large carts, instance isolation
tests/validation.test.js        Validator bounds and error messages
tests/money.test.js             Rounding and discount arithmetic
```

## Out of scope

- One algorithm for totals, not two. The guideline to implement two approaches is meant for real strategy choices, such as rate-limiting algorithms. For a cart total, a second approach would just be a way to get the same sum wrong.
- Concurrency. The cart is synchronous and single-threaded. Every method finishes before another can run, so there is nothing to interleave.
